items.title: Mortgage and Loan Insurance Programs Under the National Housing Act-Debenture Interest Rates
items.summary: This notice announces changes in the interest rates to be paid on debentures issued with respect to a loan or mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration under the provisions of the National Housing Act (the Act). The interest rate for debentures issued under Section 221(g)(4) of the Act during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4 percent. The interest rate for debentures issued under any other provision of the Act is the rate in effect on the date that the commitment to insure the loan or mortgage was issued, or the date that the loan or mortgage was endorsed (or initially endorsed if there are two or more endorsements) for insurance, whichever rate is higher. The interest rate for debentures issued under these other provisions with respect to a loan or mortgage committed or endorsed during the 6-month period beginning January 1, 2026, is 4\3/4\ percent.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Medical Equipment Suppliers (08/30/26)
story_ideas.hook: The highest-scoring item in the run is a supplier list showing what each location carries and its Medicare participation status, refreshed 08/30/26 and unmatched by any monitored publisher.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you order a walker, wheelchair, hospital bed or oxygen setup, look the supplier up and check two things: whether it carries the item you were prescribed and whether it participates in Medicare. Participation status is what decides how much of the bill lands on you, and the list is searchable down to your county.
story_ideas.b2b: For discharge planners and home health operators, the file is a referral-network audit: which suppliers within a service area actually stock the equipment being ordered at discharge, and where non-participating suppliers create surprise cost exposure that comes back as a readmission or a complaint.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to US states and counties. Coverage state is gap, so monitored publishers cover this beat and none matched the item. Clean map or county-density chart.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Provider Information (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: The file underlying the Five-Star Rating System, including certified beds, quality measure scores and staffing, was refreshed 08/01/26 with one row per nursing home.
story_ideas.consumer: A star rating is a summary of numbers you can read yourself. Pull the row for any facility you are considering and compare certified bed count, the staffing figures and the individual quality measure scores against nearby facilities, rather than stopping at the overall star.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators should expect this refresh to reset competitive positioning within their markets. The one-row-per-facility structure makes it trivial for referral sources, families and reporters to rank every building in a county on staffing, which raises the cost of a soft quarter.
story_ideas.note: State and county geography; the single strongest chart candidate in the run. Gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Penalties (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Three years of fines and payment denials received by nursing homes, refreshed 08/01/26 and not matched by any monitored publisher.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask the admissions office directly whether the facility has received a fine or a payment denial in the last three years, then verify the answer against the file. A penalty is not automatically disqualifying, but a pattern of them alongside repeat citations is a different signal than a single incident.
story_ideas.b2b: For owners and their lenders, the penalties file is a three-year liability record attached to a specific building, which matters in diligence and in insurance renewals. Pairing it with the ownership file shows whether penalties cluster within particular ownership groups rather than particular markets.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to states and counties; supports a per-facility and per-state penalty tally. Gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Ownership (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Ownership information for all currently active nursing homes was refreshed 08/01/26, alongside the quality and enforcement files.
story_ideas.consumer: The name on the sign is often not the company making decisions about staffing and spending. Look up who owns the facility, then check whether that owner runs other buildings near you and how those buildings score on the quality and deficiency files.
story_ideas.b2b: This is the M&A and consolidation dataset. Cross-referenced with the Facility Affiliation Data refreshed 07/31/26 and the penalties file, it supports a market-by-market read on which groups are growing and whether scale is tracking with quality outcomes.
story_ideas.note: State and county level; strong network-analysis and chain-ranking potential. Gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Fire Safety Deficiencies (08/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: Three years of nursing home fire safety citations, with inspection date, tag number, scope and severity, correction date and current status, refreshed 08/01/26.
story_ideas.consumer: Fire safety citations come with a scope and severity code and a correction date. Check whether an open citation at a facility you are considering has been corrected and how long the correction took, and ask the administrator to walk you through anything still outstanding.
story_ideas.b2b: Life safety code compliance is a capital planning question as much as a survey question. Buildings carrying repeat citations in the same tag categories signal deferred infrastructure spending, which is a useful screen for acquirers and for state associations mapping where older physical plants concentrate.
story_ideas.note: One citation per row, with dates and severity, so it charts cleanly over three years by state. Gap.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice care - State CAHPS Hospice Survey Data (08/07/26)
story_ideas.hook: State-level mean scores for Medicare-certified hospice providers on the CAHPS Hospice Survey were refreshed 08/07/26, paired with the national file the same day, and no monitored publisher matched either.
story_ideas.consumer: Hospice care is chosen quickly, often within days. The state survey averages tell you what families in your state reported about communication, symptom management and support, giving you a baseline to hold a specific hospice against when you interview it.
story_ideas.b2b: Hospice operators now have a refreshed state benchmark to position against in referral conversations with hospitals and skilled nursing facilities. The gap between a provider's own scores and its state mean is the number partners will ask about.
story_ideas.note: State geography, direct state-ranking chart. Sits in the palliative and hospice cluster, which holds together across 2 sources and 9 items, all 9 unmatched by monitored publishers.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services employment, August 2026 — 1,896.40 thousands of jobs (+5.0% year over year)
story_ideas.hook: Home health employment grew 5.0% year over year to 1,896.40 thousand jobs in August 2026, more than double the 2.1% growth in nursing care facilities.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are trying to stay at home, the labor market is moving your way faster than the facility market is. When you call agencies, ask specifically about current caseload capacity and how many hours per week they can guarantee, because growth in the sector nationally does not mean availability on your street.
story_ideas.b2b: The divergence between 5.0% home health growth and 2.1% nursing facility growth is a competition-for-labor story, not just a demand story. Skilled nursing and assisted living operators are hiring from the same regional pool that home care agencies are expanding into.
story_ideas.note: National series with a clean two-line year-over-year chart against the nursing care facilities figure. Gap.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings, July 2026 — 25.65 dollars per hour (+3.2% year over year)
story_ideas.hook: Average hourly earnings in assisted living and continuing care retirement communities reached $25.65 in July 2026, up 3.2%, while home health care services averaged $28.04, up 2.0%.
story_ideas.consumer: Wage costs move monthly fees. If your community raises rates this year, you can ask what share reflects direct care staffing and compare the increase against the 3.2% earnings growth in the sector, rather than accepting a single unexplained number.
story_ideas.b2b: Assisted living wages are rising faster in percentage terms than home health wages but remain $2.39 an hour below them, which is a recruitment problem for communities competing with agency work that offers more schedule control. Employment in the segment stood at 1,026.90 thousand jobs in August 2026, up 1.4%.
story_ideas.note: National only. Two-series wage chart with a visible gap; pairs with the employment figures for a single workforce package. Gap.

story_ideas.title: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services for Older Adults: A Primer (08/20/26)
story_ideas.hook: Justice in Aging published a primer on 08/20/26 explaining how Medicaid HCBS help older adults with disabilities live independently and the policy gaps limiting access.
story_ideas.consumer: If staying in your home depends on Medicaid-funded help, start by finding out what your state actually covers and whether there is a waiting list. The primer is written to explain where access breaks down, which tells you which questions to put to your state Medicaid office before you need the service.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers building home and community-based lines should treat the identified policy gaps as a market map. Where access is constrained by program design rather than demand, expansion depends on state waiver decisions, not on marketing.
story_ideas.note: Not localizable and carries no state breakouts, which makes it the interpretive spine for the data-heavy items rather than a chart. Gap.

story_ideas.title: 5 Questions and Answers About Medicaid and Provider Taxes (08/20/26)
story_ideas.hook: KFF's 08/20/26 issue brief uses its 2025-2026 survey of Medicaid directors and a proposed rule on provider taxes to describe how the rules are changing under the 2025 reconciliation law and which changes may affect each state.
story_ideas.consumer: Provider taxes are part of how your state pays for the Medicaid services that cover nursing home and home care. If your state's arrangement changes, the practical effects show up as eligibility rules, waiting lists and provider participation, so it is worth knowing where your state sits now.
story_ideas.b2b: For nursing home and LTSS operators, provider tax rules are a direct reimbursement variable. The state-by-state summary is the planning document for budget cycles, and the survey of Medicaid directors indicates where administrators expect the pressure to land.
story_ideas.note: No geographic breakouts flagged in the item, but the brief itself summarizes state-level effects. Sits in the Medicare and Medicaid group, which does not cohere. Gap.

story_ideas.title: American Community Survey 2023 state aging and housing profile (52 states)
story_ideas.hook: State-level 2023 ACS 5-year estimates cover 65+, 65-74, 75-84 and 85+ populations with median household income and housing tenure, including 5,994,486 residents aged 65 and over in California and 4,630,733 in Florida.
story_ideas.consumer: Compare your state's older population and median household income against the states your family is considering for a move or for caregiving proximity. The 85+ count is the number that predicts how strained local care capacity will be by the time you need it.
story_ideas.b2b: For senior housing developers and operators, the 75-84 and 85+ splits paired with housing tenure and median income are the demand and affordability screen for site selection. Owner-occupancy rates tell you how much home equity is available to convert into entry fees.
story_ideas.localize: Breaks down to US states — rank the outliers.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.note: All 52 state-level units, the most directly rankable item in the run and the base layer for any localized version. Gap.

story_ideas.title: Fair Market Rents for the Housing Choice Voucher Program, Moderate Rehabilitation Single Room Occupancy Program, and Other Programs, Fiscal Year 2027 (09/01/26)
story_ideas.hook: HUD published FY 2027 Fair Market Rents on 09/01/26, effective October 1, along with the procedures for public housing agencies to request reevaluations under HOTMA.
story_ideas.consumer: If you use a Housing Choice Voucher, the amount it covers changes on October 1. Check the new FMR for your area now and, if it looks out of line with what units actually rent for, ask your public housing agency whether it intends to request a reevaluation.
story_ideas.b2b: Affordable senior housing operators and nonprofit sponsors should model FY 2027 FMRs against their rent rolls before October 1. The reevaluation procedure is the only in-year correction available, and it runs through the PHA, not the property.
story_ideas.note: Effective date creates a hard news peg. Pairs with the Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice published 09/04/26, the newest item in the run. Both are gaps.

trends_raw: Volume held essentially flat at 169 evidence candidates against 170 on 09/03/26, with nothing first surfacing in this run, so today's shape reflects what is maturing rather than what just arrived. Housing and financial security each gained an item, and both gains are regulatory: the Housing Trust Fund FY 2026 allocation notice on 09/04/26 and the FY 2027 Fair Market Rents notice on 09/01/26, with Social Security Ruling SSR 26-2p also dated 09/01/26. Long-term care and Medicare and Medicaid each shed one. Medicare and Medicaid is the busiest beat with 29 items drawn from seven sources including ACL, CMS, the Federal Register, KFF and Justice in Aging, but it is not one story; those items share a tag and little else, ranging from a device coverage pathway to rural maternity access to provider taxes. Long-term care, at 18 items, does hold together, which is why it carries the feature. Palliative and hospice care is the tightest cluster in the run at 9 items from CMS provider data and RAND, with all 9 unmatched. Housing at 14, workforce at 12 and financial security at 11 fill out the volume. Coverage posture is unusually open: 84 confirmed gaps where monitored publishers work the beat and none matched the item, and 76 items on beats where no monitored publisher is being watched at all, which says nothing about whether anyone else has covered them. The publishers found reporting anything in this run — including the American Hospital Association, Nature and Pharmacy Times — sit outside the aging trade entirely, which is consistent with a run dominated by refreshed federal datasets that clinical and general outlets touch and the aging press has not yet worked.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** On 08/01/26 CMS refreshed nearly the entire public accountability record for nursing homes in a single pass — Provider Information (the file behind the Five-Star Rating System), Health Deficiencies, Fire Safety Deficiencies, Penalties, Ownership, Survey Summary, Inspection Dates, Citation Code Look-up, Nursing Home Data Collection Intervals, MDS Quality Measures, Medicare Claims Quality Measures and the Skilled Nursing Facility Quality Reporting Program provider file. BLS put nursing care facilities employment at 1,590.20 thousand jobs in August 2026, up 2.1% year over year, against home health care services at 1,896.40 thousand, up 5.0%. Justice in Aging's 08/20/26 primer on Medicaid home and community-based services lays out the policy gaps that limit access to the community alternative, and the Center for Retirement Research's 09/03/26 comparison of long-term care in Israel and the United States puts the same structural problem in relief. The substantive thread is an accountability asymmetry: the institutional side of long-term care is the most exhaustively documented and the slowest-growing, while the home-based side families are steered toward is growing more than twice as fast with far less published about who delivers it and how well.

**Why pitch this now:** KFF's 08/20/26 brief on Medicaid and provider taxes describes rules changing under the 2025 reconciliation law and the regulations implementing it, and summarizes which changes may affect each state. Medicaid is the payer standing behind much of this care, and the financing under it is moving this fiscal year. The CMS files are current as of 08/01/26 and carry state and county geography, so a state-level read is available before those changes land.

**Angle:** "The Paper Trail Your Nursing Home Leaves" — a families-choosing-a-facility explainer built on the refreshed CMS files, with a companion trade read on why the documented side of the sector is the one adding the fewest workers.

**Potential headlines:**
- What CMS Just Published About Every Nursing Home in Your State
- Nursing Home Jobs Grew 2.1 Percent While Home Care Grew 5 Percent
- The Fines, Citations and Owners Behind a Five Star Rating

**Potential outlets:**
- Kiplinger — retirement economics and long-term care costs, with an appetite for state comparisons the CMS county-level files support.
- SeniorLiving.org — a consumer senior-living audience actively shopping facilities, and a natural home for a state-ranking treatment.
- Family Caregiver Alliance — caregiver readers making placement decisions who need the deficiency and penalty files translated into questions to ask.
- McKnight's Long-Term Care News — the core skilled nursing audience for a quality-data and staffing story.
- Skilled Nursing News — original data with direct business implications, especially the ownership file paired with employment growth.
- Provider Magazine — strong on Medicaid, staffing and state-by-state data, which is exactly where the provider-tax context lands.
